content: Mass media interventions are a method of delivering preventive health messages to the public. These interventions have the potential to influence the knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors of a large segment of the population. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of mass media campaigns in preventing smoking among young people under the age of 25. Specifically, the review aimed to determine whether these campaigns could reduce smoking initiation, improve attitudes and intentions regarding smoking, enhance knowledge about smoking risks, boost self-efficacy and self-esteem, and positively influence perceptions about smoking, including encouraging young people to follow positive role models. The review included randomized trials, non-randomized controlled trials, and interrupted time-series studies that assessed the impact of mass media campaigns on smoking behavior. Mass media campaigns were defined as communication strategies using channels such as television, radio, newspapers, social media, billboards, posters, leaflets, or booklets, designed to reach large audiences without relying on direct person-to-person contact. Smoking behavior was defined as the presence or absence of tobacco use, the type of tobacco used, and the frequency of use. Comparators included educational interventions or no intervention at all. The authors conducted a systematic search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, and Embase, with the most recent search performed in June 2016. This review is an update of a previous review first published in 1998. Two independent reviewers extracted data on the characteristics of the interventions, participants, outcomes, study methods, and risks of bias. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and the risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool, with additional criteria tailored to the nature of the interventions. The review identified eight eligible studies, including one new study added in this update. Seven studies employed a controlled trial design, while one used an interrupted time-series analysis. The studies exhibited high risks of bias and significant heterogeneity in terms of design, intervention characteristics, and populations studied. Three studies (n = 17,385) reported that mass media interventions reduced smoking behavior among young people. Of these, one study compared a mass media campaign to no intervention, while two studies evaluated mass media campaigns as adjuncts to school-based interventions. In contrast, five studies (n = 72,740) did not find a significant effect on smoking behavior. These included three studies comparing mass media campaigns to no intervention, one study assessing a mass media campaign as an adjunct to a school-based intervention, and one interrupted time-series study focusing on a social media intervention. The campaigns that demonstrated significant effects shared certain characteristics. They were grounded in theoretical frameworks, utilized formative research to design campaign messages, and delivered messages with sufficient intensity over extended periods. Effective campaigns typically lasted at least three years and involved intensive exposure, such as a minimum of eight school-based lessons per grade and media spots lasting at least four weeks across multiple channels, with between 167 and 350 television and radio spots. Successful campaigns also incorporated school-based components, such as posters, and employed repetitive messaging across various media platforms, including newspapers, radio, and television. However, some campaigns that did not show significant effects also exhibited these characteristics, highlighting the inconsistency in findings. The authors concluded that the certainty regarding the effectiveness of mass media campaigns in preventing smoking among youth is very low. This uncertainty is due to inconsistencies in study designs and results, as well as methodological limitations in the included studies. As a result, it is not possible to draw firm conclusions from the current evidence. The authors emphasized the need for methodologically rigorous studies to evaluate the impact of social media and emerging technologies as part of tobacco prevention campaigns targeting young people.
